extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for organizing, governing, and instructing a common (primary) school: how to introduce limited pupil self-government, prioritize fundamental skills, arrange classes, and balance recitation with instruction. Emphasis is on gradual implementation, systematization, and methods for acting on numbers of pupils at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher retains practical control over student self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: When adopting plans of self-government, the teacher must possess such a share of 'generalship' that he can really manage the institution himself while the power is nominally and apparently in the hands of the pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the teacher's personal influence remains strong; if the teacher loses influence and the institution is really surrendered to pupils, the plan is on unstable footing and likely to be abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and restrict pupil decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Call upon pupils to act upon and decide questions relative to the school only within such limits and under such restrictions as may appear best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pupil decision-making to interest them and secure cooperation, teach self-control and submission to the majority; do not give unrestricted authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce pupil power gradually and by small experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid formal sudden announcements of giving pupils power; prepare them gradually for power and let them exercise it only so far as they are prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a simple delegated task (e.g., distributing writing-books), test it for a short term (one week), thank participants, then extend if successful. Never make large-scale innovations abruptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select pleasant and popular initial office-holders
rubrics_metrics.description: When nominating pupils to small offices, select pleasant and popular boys who will gladly assist and be agreeable to their schoolmates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity and agreeableness are necessary for securing success; include sometimes a boy not friendly to the teacher to gain influence, but appoint only as circumstances warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use committees and officers to organize school business
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize pupils into committees and appoint officers (secretary, distributors, committee for fire, etc.) to handle various departments of business, making the school regularly organized as a society or legislative assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by dictating duties and records, then gradually require more independence (e.g., secretary begins by copying dictated notes, later records independently). Use committees for counting, reporting, assigning, and maintaining order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use calm, delayed review to discipline misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A calm review of misconduct after the excitement has gone by will do more to bring it into disgrace than violent invectives and reproaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When incidents occur, defer harsh treatment until tempers cool; narrate facts impartially to the whole school to show necessity of remedies without naming culprits or reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a safe, accessible channel for complaints and propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a small wrapper or box where any pupil may write a 'proposition' (motion, complaint, or question) to be brought to the teacher at the appointed time for business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read propositions aloud; some cases may be referred to scholars for decision, some decided by the teacher, others set aside. The wrapper acts as a safety valve and thermometer of school opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit time devoted to pupil government business
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against allowing arrangements of pupil government to occupy too much time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From experience, about fifteen minutes each day with a school of 135 is enough; this ought never to be exceeded to avoid loss of instructional time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent office duties from harming scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid appointing pupils to offices who will neglect their studies; office-holders must be good scholars, punctual, and prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an office-holder falls behind, kindly suggest resignation and trial without office; insist on resignation if necessary. A few decided cases will remove the evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and remove insubordination promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: If pupils show discontent or murmur when their decisions are not followed or when restricted, this spirit must be immediately and decidedly checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pose direct questions to the school to demonstrate the impracticality of full student government; explain that trustees hold the teacher responsible and the teacher must retain ultimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain limits of delegated authority clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it clear to pupils that while their opinions are sometimes solicited, the teacher retains the ultimate authority and only delegates what he chooses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between asking for the scholars' wishes to help the teacher decide and actually surrendering final control; guard against pupils assuming full republican control of the school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act upon system: classify particulars and assign time
rubrics_metrics.description: In making general arrangements, look carefully over the ground, consider objects to accomplish, and the proper degree of time and attention each deserves; act upon system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange and classify particulars that would otherwise crowd in confusion; assign each to its proper time and place so your time is under your command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate trust according to demonstrated capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegate power as freely as possible, but only as far as pupils show themselves capable of exercising it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest pupils by reposing trust in them where they prove able; gradually extend responsibilities as they demonstrate readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about innovations; test small then extend
rubrics_metrics.description: Make no rash experiments on a large scale; always test new measures in a small way and gradually extend them if they prove good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce practices like propositions or officers only as fast as actually needed and only after initial small successful trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize the three fundamental branches: Reading, Writing, Calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading, Writing, and Calculation are distinct arts and the foundational means by which all other knowledge is acquired; they stand first in importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim primarily to make all pupils good readers, writers, and calculators; consider other studies chiefly as practice in applying these arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey the whole school to assess proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: At the start, make an estimate of the state of your pupils in reading, writing, and arithmetic — e.g., have all write a specimen, let all read, assess arithmetic ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note how many read fluently, with difficulty, or only letters; how many can perform elementary arithmetic; use this survey to form a plan to elevate the whole mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form individual plans based on each pupil's stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain, by informal means, to what stage each pupil's education has advanced and deliberately consider what objectives you can reasonably hope to effect for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use individual assessments to modify general plans and keep work systematic rather than random.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply teaching power by acting on numbers at once
rubrics_metrics.description: The great business of public instruction is the teacher's skill in multiplying his power by acting on numbers at a time (classes, groups), not only on individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and arrange numbers with varied knowledge and capacity to carry them forward together; recognize theoretical limits (e.g., many hundreds can hear an explanation) but arrange practicably to reduce waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and minimize waste when teaching small groups
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving special attention to two or three individuals, be conscious that much of your labor may only affect that small portion rather than the whole class — avoid this waste when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape measures to diminish loss of instructional reach; plan how to bring idle 'power' (unused capacity) into practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and balance Recitation and Instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation (examination of individuals to secure faithful performance of tasks) and Instruction (explanation, assistance, additional information) are distinct and both must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid class meetings that are mere mechanical recitations (which kill literary spirit) or mere instruction without examination (which becomes a lecture). Use both so pupils are prepared and genuinely learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure recitation verifies preparation using time-efficient methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher must in some way satisfy himself by reasonable evidence that the whole class are really prepared; ingenuity is needed to effect this in the shortest possible time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: instead of calling one word to one pupil (inefficient), require all to write dictated spelling words on slates and then spell simultaneously, marking errors — teacher glances at slates to identify who needs further inspection.
